destination.title: The Supreme Court Let Police Take Your DNA at Arrest

short13: Get arrested, even by mistake, and police can take your DNA, and keep it.
In 2009, a man was arrested for assault.
At booking, they swabbed the inside of his cheek.
That sample matched an unsolved case from years earlier.
It looks like justice, but here's the catch.
In 2013, the Supreme Court called it legal, just like fingerprints.
But four justices, left and right, dissented: it's a search of your body for crimes you're not even suspected of.
Watch the full story on the channel.

candidate_payload_lines: In 2013, by a single vote, the Supreme Court said they are allowed to do that.

The question in this case was whether a DNA swab belongs in that box — a routine way to identify you — or whether it is something else: a search of your body for evidence of crimes no one has accused you of.
In 2009, a man named Alonzo King is arrested in Maryland.
And there, it matches genetic evidence left at the scene of a rape from 2003 — a case that had gone unsolved for years .
In 2013, the Supreme Court upheld the swab.
Each time, a power that began small is stretched to fit a world the founders never saw — and each time, a court has to decide how far is too far.
Can they come in after you, without a warrant?

shorts.angle: The majority's whole case rests on one word, identification, and Justice Kennedy defined it far more broadly than your name.
shorts.avoids: The existing Short states the outcome, that the Court called the swab legal just like fingerprints; this cut opens the majority's reasoning and shows what the word doing that work actually meant.
shorts.funnel_question_left_for_longform: Why did the Court's most conservative justice and three of its most liberal justices end up on the same side against that definition?
shorts.loop_join: L5 leaves the majority's definition in force, so L1 returns as current practice, which is why that one word carries the whole thing.

lines.text: Police can swab your DNA at booking because the Supreme Court called it identification. That word does not mean what you think it means.
source_lines: In 2013, by a single vote, the Supreme Court said they are allowed to do that.

lines.text: Fingerprints are allowed at booking for one reason. Their purpose is confirming that the person in the cell is who they say they are.
source_lines: Courts have long allowed this, because its purpose is identification — confirming that the person in the cell is who they say they are, and checking whether they are wanted elsewhere

lines.text: Justice Kennedy said identification meant more than a name. Knowing an arrestee's full history helps officers judge how dangerous he might be.
source_lines: Kennedy also spelled out what "identification" meant to the majority, and it was broader than a name.
Knowing an arrestee's full history, the Court said, helps officers judge how dangerous he might be, whether he is a flight risk, and whether he threatens the people around him.

lines.text: Whether he is a flight risk. Whether he threatens the people around him. On that reading the swab was not a fishing expedition. It was processing.
source_lines: DNA, in that view, was not a fishing expedition — it was part of safely processing a person already in the state's custody

lines.text: The database has a name, CODIS, the FBI's national DNA index. The whole value of swabbing arrestees comes from searching it against cold cases.
source_lines: CODIS, the FBI's national DNA index
and the whole value of swabbing arrestees comes from searching it against cold cases

lines.text: Scalia answered that the police already knew who King was. The purpose was investigating unsolved crimes, which the Constitution forbids without suspicion.
source_lines: The swab, he said, was not really about identifying Alonzo King
Its purpose was to investigate unsolved crimes, and the Constitution does not allow the government to search a person for evidence of crime without a reason to suspect them of it

lines.text: He warned that a person's DNA can be taken and entered into a national database if they are ever arrested, rightly or wrongly.
source_lines: as a consequence of this decision, he wrote, your DNA can be taken and entered into a national DNA database if you are ever arrested, rightly or wrongly, and for whatever reason

lines.text: The four in dissent lost, which means the definition in the majority opinion is the one police work from today.

shorts.angle: A fingerprint reveals a pattern, while a DNA sample is a blueprint of your relatives and your health, and the state keeps the sample itself.
shorts.avoids: The existing Short accepts the Court's fingerprint comparison and moves straight to the vote; this cut measures the distance between the two things being compared.
shorts.funnel_question_left_for_longform: If the law reads only a narrow set of markers today, who decides when that limit moves?
shorts.loop_join: L5 makes everything turn on what a swab takes, and L1 hands back the Court's own answer, the fingerprint comparison, for a second look.

lines.text: The Supreme Court compared a DNA swab to a fingerprint. Look at how far apart those two things actually are.
source_lines: In 2013, the Supreme Court upheld the swab.
It is, in the Court's words, like fingerprinting and photographing — a legitimate booking procedure

lines.text: A fingerprint reveals almost nothing about you except its own pattern. DNA is a blueprint that can expose your relatives, your health, your most private traits.
source_lines: A fingerprint reveals almost nothing about you except its own pattern. DNA is different — it is a blueprint that can expose your relatives, your health, your most private traits.

lines.text: The majority answered that the law reads only a narrow set of identifying markers, not your whole genome. That was the promise.
source_lines: The majority stressed that the law used only a narrow set of identifying markers, not your whole genome.

lines.text: But critics answered that the physical sample itself is kept. And that the line the state draws today, it can quietly move tomorrow.
source_lines: Critics answered that the physical sample itself is kept, and that the line the state draws today, it can quietly move tomorrow

lines.text: In much of the country, being arrested for a serious offense now means giving a sample before any trial, and it is kept.
source_lines: In much of the country, being arrested for a serious offense now means giving a DNA sample

lines.text: The people swept into those databases include the merely arrested, whose genetic code is on file because of a single encounter with the police.
source_lines: the people swept into those databases include the merely arrested
whose genetic code is now on file because of a single encounter with the police

lines.text: The other side is real. DNA databases have closed cold cases, freed innocent people, and identified violent offenders who would otherwise have walked free.
source_lines: The system genuinely works: DNA databases have closed cold cases, freed innocent people, and identified violent offenders who would otherwise have walked free

lines.text: The Court weighed that risk against a public interest and called the swab reasonable. Whether that holds depends on what you think a swab actually takes.
